subject: science
passage: In the 1880s, meteorologists in India noticed that winters with unusually heavy snow in the Himalayas tended to be followed by weak summer monsoons. The idea makes physical sense: snow-covered land reflects sunlight and spends energy on melting, so it warms slowly in spring, weakening the land-sea temperature contrast that draws moist ocean air inland. Climatologist Priya Raghavan argues that Eurasian snow cover therefore remains one of the most dependable signals for forecasting the monsoon.
passage_b: The link between snow and the monsoon is physically plausible, and in some decades it has held up well. But a forecasting signal is only as good as its consistency, and this one has been erratic: in several recent decades the correlation between spring snow cover and monsoon rainfall weakened or nearly vanished, apparently because other influences, such as conditions in the tropical Pacific, came to dominate. A link that fades and returns cannot be called dependable.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the argument made by Raghavan in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that the tropical Pacific is the only reliable guide to monsoon rainfall
choices.B: By claiming that heavy Himalayan snow is usually followed by unusually strong monsoons
choices.C: By rejecting the physical explanation of how snow cover could weaken the monsoon
choices.D: By granting that the link is plausible but denying that it is a dependable signal

explanation.why: Text 2 opens by calling the snow-monsoon link "physically plausible," so it accepts the reasoning in Text 1. It then argues that the correlation has "weakened or nearly vanished" in recent decades and concludes that such a link "cannot be called dependable," which is the very word Raghavan uses. Text 2 accepts the mechanism but rejects the claim of reliability.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 mentions the tropical Pacific only as one of the "other influences"; it never calls it the only reliable guide.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 never claims that heavy snow leads to strong monsoons; it says only that the snow-monsoon correlation has been inconsistent.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 calls the link "physically plausible," so it does not reject the explanation.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 accepts that the link makes physical sense but says its inconsistency in recent decades keeps it from being a dependable signal.
